paper_title: From VLM Planners to Robotic Agents: Self-Evolving Harnesses for History-Dependent Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance across embodied manipulation tasks by unifying visual understanding, language conditioning, and action generation. However, long-horizon tasks can involve non-Markovian dependencies: successful decisions may require retaining task progress and past interaction outcomes, while partial observability and execution errors compound over time. Existing work has begun to address these challenges by augmenting foundation-model policies with memory and by introducing hierarchical architectures that separate high-level planning from low-level execution. We organize the high-level VLM as a robotic agent through an editable harness to maintain task context and improve planning through execution experience. We instantiate this approach as SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), with a fixed VLA executor providing low-level control. The harness maintains and updates task context using observations and execution feedback to guide subsequent planning. Self-evolution uses environment rollouts to propose and evaluate harness revisions, with the selected configuration fixed before held-out testing. On RoboMME, SERA achieves 51.38% overall success with autonomous selection, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. Our exploration suggests that agentic planning is a promising direction for history-dependent robotic manipulation.

sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance across embodied manipulation tasks by unifying visual understanding, language conditioning, and action generation. Existing work has begun to address these challenges by augmenting foundation-model policies with memory and by introducing hierarchical architectures that separate high-level planning from low-level execution. We organize the high-level VLM as robotic agent through an editable harness to maintain task context and improve planning through execution experience. We instantiate this approach as SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), with fixed VLA executor providing low-level control. The harness maintains and updates task context using observations and execution feedback to guide subsequent planning. Self-evolution uses environment rollouts to propose and evaluate harness revisions, with the selected configuration fixed before held-out testing. On RoboMME, SERA achieves 51.38% overall success with autonomous selection, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. Our exploration suggests that agentic planning is promising direction for history-dependent robotic manipulation.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, providing foundation for general-purpose manipulation (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024). Long-horizon tasks, however, can require information that the current observation does not reveal (Koo et al., 2025; Dai et al., 2026). For example, when robot must repeat an operation specified number of times, similar images may call for different decisions depending on how many repetitions have actually succeeded. An earlier observation may also contain cue that is no longer visible. Such history-dependent decisions require preserving task-relevant information and tracking execution outcomes over successive interactions. Existing research provides several foundations for these capabilities. Memory-augmented policies equip VLA models with mechanisms for retaining and using historical information, including compact temporal representations (Koo et al., 2025; Jang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026), memory retrieval, and recurrent state updates (Shi et al., 2025a; Hu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). Hierarchical architectures introduce high-level planning layer that issues intermediate decisions to low-level executors (Ahn et al., 2022; Belkhale et al., 2024; Duan et al., 2025; Sridhar et al., 2025) and can incorporate environment feedback (Huang et al., 2022). Agentic systems further organize reasoning, actions, and feedback into iterative decision processes (Yao et al., 2022; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023). Recent embodied harnesses explore external task management (Zhang et al., 2026b; Gu et al., 2026) 1 Preprint Figure 1: From planner to agent for history-dependent manipulation. Top: Similar observations can require different decisions depending on task progress. (a) Memory-augmented policies equip VLA models with memory mechanisms to retain and use historical information. (b) Hierarchical planning separates high-level planning from low-level execution. (c) SERA uses an editable harness to organize the VLM as an agent that maintains task context from observation and interaction history. Execution-driven self-evolution refines the harness using rollout feedback. The dashed arrow denotes the selected harness, fixed before testing. and experience-driven adaptation (Chen et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2026). Together, these developments motivate studying how the high-level planner in hierarchical architecture can manage task context and make use of execution experience. Our focus is on two connected responsibilities of this planning process. Within an episode, issuing command does not establish that the intended operation has succeeded. In the repetition example, updating progress requires interpreting subsequent observations and feedback, while retaining information needed for later decisions. Access to history therefore needs to be accompanied by an explicit process for maintaining decision-relevant task context. Across attempts, an execution record must be translated into reusable change to influence future planning. This raises question: how can we support both ongoing context management and improvements to the planning process from execution experience? We explore an editable harness around the high-level VLM as common mechanism for these responsibilities. The harness organizes context and feedback during execution, while providing an explicit object for revision during self-evolution. This also offers way to investigate experience reuse when additional demonstrations and manual annotations are costly. Figure 1 illustrates this design direction. We present SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), which organizes VLM as an agent within an editable harness around fixed VLA executor. During task execution, the harness supports sustained context management over long horizons, guiding the extraction, retention, and updating of task progress and execution outcomes from observations and feedback. This context supports the VLMs subsequent planning. However, predefined harness may not anticipate all task requirements, motivating execution-driven self-evolution to identify and repair its limitations. Analysis and revision agents autonomously diagnose failures from execution traces and propose candidate repairs to planning guidance, assessment criteria, and control rules. verifier evaluates these candidates through environment rollouts, providing feedback for further revision and harness selection. This process revises the harness without manually constructing additional demonstration datasets for su2 Preprint pervised fine-tuning of the high-level VLM planner. The selected harness is fixed before held-out testing, while task context continues to be updated within each episode. We evaluate SERA on RoboMME, benchmark for history-dependent robotic manipulation (Dai et al., 2026). Autonomous SERA achieves 51.38% overall success, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. These results support an empirical exploration of agentic planning and the aggregate effect of execution-driven harness revisions. Our contributions are: An agentic planning framework that organizes high-level VLM within an editable harness for sustained task-context management over long horizons, tracking task progress and execution feedback to guide fixed VLA executor. An execution-driven self-evolution procedure that autonomously proposes and evaluates revisions to planning guidance, assessment criteria, and control rules from rollout feedback, without constructing an SFT dataset. We evaluate SERA on RoboMME and achieve 51.38% overall success. Harness selfevolution improves success by 7.00 percentage points over the initial configuration.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: 2.1 MEMORY-AUGMENTED POLICIES Generalist robot policies learn language-conditioned manipulation from diverse data (Brohan et al., 2022; Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2023; Octo Model Team et al., 2024). VLA models connect pretrained vision-language representations with action learning (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025). Related embodied models, including PaLM-E, incorporate visual and continuous state inputs into language models for embodied reasoning and planning (Driess et al., 2023). These developments provide foundation for language-conditioned manipulation, while history-dependent tasks additionally require information beyond the current observation. Recent work has also emphasized the importance of historical information in manipulation, with benchmarks such as RoboMME explicitly evaluating history-dependent behavior (Dai et al., 2026). Memory-augmented policies incorporate such information through different representations and update mechanisms (Fang et al., 2025). HAMLET aggregates compact moment tokens across timesteps to condition action prediction (Koo et al., 2025). MemoryVLA retrieves perceptual and cognitive information from memory bank and fuses it with current representations (Shi et al., 2025a), while ContextVLA compresses past observations into context token for efficient multiframe conditioning (Jang et al., 2025). Other designs address cross-subtask information transfer through event-triggered latent memory in WeaveLA (Zhu et al., 2026), hierarchical experience retrieval in ECHO (Hu et al., 2026), and temporal aggregation through frameand chunk-level recurrent queries in ReMem-VLA (Li et al., 2026). These methods integrate historical information into action prediction through compact temporal representations, memory retrieval, or recurrent updates. 2.2 HIERARCHICAL ROBOTIC PLANNING Hierarchical approaches connect high-level reasoning to executable robot behavior through intermediate decisions (Rana et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026a). SayCan combines language-model planning with affordance estimates for pretrained skills (Ahn et al., 2022), and Inner Monologue incorporates environment feedback into subsequent planning (Huang et al., 2022). Code as Policies expresses robot behavior as programs invoking perception and control APIs (Liang et al., 2022). Other interfaces include the spatial value maps of VoxPoser, the relational keypoint constraints of ReKep, and the language motions of RT-H (Huang et al., 2023; 2024; Belkhale et al., 2024). RoboPARA further uses dependency graphs and resource constraints to organize parallel dual-arm execution (Duan et al., 2025). Memory and hierarchical planning can also be combined. MemER trains high-level VLM to nominate historical keyframes and predict language subtasks; selected keyframes inform subsequent decisions, while low-level VLA executes the subtasks (Sridhar et al., 2025). Goal2Skill combines 3 Preprint structured task memory with subtask verification and replanning in VLMVLA hierarchy (Liu et al., 2026). 2.3 AGENTIC EMBODIED SYSTEMS AND SELF-EVOLUTION Research on language models and agents studies reasoning, interaction, and feedback-driven refinement (Madaan et al., 2023). ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions and observations (Yao et al., 2022); Reflexion stores textual feedback for subsequent attempts (Shinn et al., 2023); and Voyager accumulates reusable executable skills through interaction in Minecraft (Wang et al., 2023). Related methods improve prompts or agent code using execution feedback (Agrawal et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). These works provide precedents for agent loops and experience reuse, although their evaluation settings differ from robotic manipulation. Recent embodied systems place these ideas around learned executors (Ahn et al., 2024). Harness VLA combines frozen VLA primitive with analytic primitives and task-specific and global memories (Zhang et al., 2026b). HarnessWAM maintains evidence-grounded task state and task graph, and compiles plans into capability-constrained WAM skills (Gu et al., 2026). RoboMemory combines spatial, temporal, episodic, and semantic memories with plannercritic loop (Lei et al., 2025). HELM couples episodic memory with learned state verifier and recovery control around frozen VLA (Zeng et al., 2026). Cortex combines task-context memory and skill constraints in deployment harness (Peng et al., 2026). Execution-driven harness adaptation is also an emerging research direction. ETA studies experiencederived strategy and skill updates subject to runtime checks before promotion (Chen et al., 2026). SHAPER evolves textual skills and context-code harness using rollout feedback and validation while keeping its planner and executor frozen (Wang et al., 2026). Zetta revises runtime critics, recovery playbooks, and executable tools from failed rollouts (Ding et al., 2026). Within this line of work, SERA explores an editable harness for high-level planning in history-dependent robotic manipulation. The harness supports within-episode context management and is revised using development-stage execution experience, with the selected version fixed before testing.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: 3.1 PROBLEM FORMULATION We consider history-dependent robotic manipulation tasks specified by language instruction i. Each episode may provide initial context c0, such as demonstration or previously observed events. At policy query time t, the robot receives sensory observation ot, and the policy predicts an action chunk At. The decision problem is non-Markovian with respect to the instantaneous observation: similar current observations can require different actions depending on earlier interactions. For example, the correct placement target may depend on the order in which locations were visited in an earlier demonstration, which cannot be inferred from the current observation alone. We define the interaction history ht and predicted action chunk At as ht = (c0, o0, a0, . . . , at1, ot), At = (at, . . . , at+K1), (1) where is the prediction horizon and aj is control action. The objective is to complete the task within bounded interaction budget using history-conditioned policy, At π( i, ht). SERA maintains an explicit task context alongside recent observations to make past information available for high-level planning. This context is an approximate record of task state and is updated as new execution evidence arrives. (2) 3.2 AGENTIC HARNESS FOR PLANNING Framework overview. SERA organizes high-level VLM as an agent through an editable harness, with fixed VLA executor for low-level control. We denote the harness configuration by H: it specifies how inputs are assembled, task context is maintained, commands are checked, and execution feedback is used in subsequent decisions. Figure 2(a) shows the resulting planningexecution 4 Preprint Figure 2: Agentic execution and harness self-evolution. (a) The harness maintains task context and uses VLM to plan commands for VLA executor, incorporating execution feedback in subsequent rounds. (b) Execution traces guide revisions to planning guidance, assessment criteria, and control rules. verifier evaluates candidates and informs further revision and selection; the selected harness is fixed before testing. Tokens denote information categories and image stacks show observation sequences. loop. Execution-driven self-evolution revises using rollout feedback, without requiring additional training of the VLM planner (Section 3.3). Episode initialization and task context. At initialization, the harness derives episode guidance g, including task description, from the instruction and initial context c0. This guidance remains fixed within the episode. During execution, the harness updates the task context cn using recent observations and execution feedback. The context contains compact summary of task progress, decision-relevant facts, execution outcomes, and unresolved uncertainty, together with control state for tracking lack of progress. By retaining relevant information after its supporting images leave the recent observation window, the context makes earlier events available to later planning. Initialization priors and context fields are detailed in Appendix B.2. Context-aware planning. At planning round n, the harness provides the VLM with g, recent visual observations Vn, runtime context cn, and the previously executed command un1. To support command generation, it also supplies action candidates Acand,n from the executors supported command set. These candidates specify available commands and their required arguments. Candidate retrieval and command-format details are given in Appendix B.1. The VLM uses the observations to assess the effect of the previous command, then proposes an updated context and high-level command in the same call. Action-specific assessment criteria, when available, guide attention to relevant execution evidence. The harness checks the response and applies its execution-control rules before storing the resulting context and issuing the command. The combined update is (cn+1, un) = PH (g, Vn, cn, un1; Acand,n). (3) Here, PH includes both the VLM call and the surrounding harness operations; un is the command actually passed to the executor. The first round uses an initial context and no preceding command. 5 Preprint Execution and feedback. The harness converts un into the executors required input format. Let xt denote the executors native conditioning inputs, including its observations and any required task or history inputs. At the policy query time tn for planning round n, the VLA with fixed parameters θ predicts an action chunk, Atn πθ( xtn, un). (4) The execution loop applies bounded prefix of this chunk over multiple control steps and collects the resulting observations. After this execution interval, the harness starts the next planning round unless the episode terminates or exhausts its budget. Each round queries the VLA once; the same subtask can continue across rounds with newly predicted chunks. The next round combines this execution evidence with the retained context to decide whether to continue, advance, or recover missing prerequisite. Harness control state tracks repeated uncertain or stagnant outcomes and can request reconsideration or another command selection. Context and control details appear in Appendix B.2; the runtime context is reset between episodes. 3.3 EXECUTION-DRIVEN SELF-EVOLUTION predefined harness may not anticipate all task requirements, leading to recurring errors in progress tracking, command selection, or recovery. Execution-driven self-evolution uses environment rollouts to identify and revise these limitations. Starting from H0, analysis and revision agents propose candidate harness changes, and verifier supplies feedback for further revision and selection (Figure 2(b)). This process changes the procedure that maintains and uses task context, beyond updating the context of an individual episode. Failure diagnosis. An analysis agent examines recorded observations, task context, issued commands, and outcomes to identify where execution first diverged from the intended behavior. It considers physical execution and task-progress reasoning separately, tracing their relationship to the terminal failure. The diagnosis specifies repair target, supporting evidence, uncertainty, and task scope, forming hypothesis for subsequent rollout evaluation. Offline diagnostic materials and restrictions on deployable repair triggers are specified in Appendix B.3. Candidate harness revisions. revision agent translates the diagnosis into candidate bundle with activation conditions and intended behavioral changes. Candidates can revise three parts of H: planning guidance directs the VLMs planning and recovery; assessment criteria specify evidence for judging execution outcomes; and control rules govern recovery and task transitions. Here, planning guidance refers to procedural instructions in the harness, while denotes the episode guidance established at initialization. The harness incorporates candidate changes into prompt construction and runtime control, allowing the candidate to alter the execution loop in Section 3.2. The revision process operates on these external components without constructing an additional demonstration dataset for supervised fine-tuning of the high-level VLM planner. Candidate revisions are expressed as structured updates to supported harness components. They can change the guidance supplied to the planner or activate registered runtime control mechanisms, while preserving the executors command interface. This constrains the repair process to changes the execution loop can apply and inspect. Verification and iterative revision. verifier evaluates candidate harnesses through environment rollouts. For given repair target, it compares candidate outcomes with cached baseline outcomes on the same evaluation episodes, recording repaired failures, regressed successes, and unchanged outcomes. subsequent review examines whether the intervention activated and how it affected execution. These findings guide another revision, different repair target, or rejection within the search budget. Candidates meeting the initial evaluation criteria can be assessed on additional episodes excluded from their diagnosis and revision. Panel construction and selection rules are described in Appendix B.3. Selection and deployment. The autonomous selection procedure allows both candidates passing fresh validation and eligible fallbacks retained when the search budget is exhausted; tasks without selected revision retain the base harness (Appendix B.3). The selected configuration is fixed before held-out testing, and test outcomes do not enter its revision process. During testing, task context cn continues to update, while and executor parameters θ remain fixed. 6 Preprint

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate SERA on RoboMME to examine agentic planning on history-dependent tasks and execution-driven harness repair, combining aggregate results with execution cases. We then discuss directions for improving execution reliability. 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Benchmark and metric. RoboMME (Dai et al., 2026) contains 16 history-dependent manipulation tasks in four suites: Counting, Permanence, Reference, and Imitation. We evaluate each SERA configuration on 50 episodes per task, totaling 800 episodes. Success rate (SR) is averaged equally across tasks within each suite and across all 16 tasks for the overall score. Appendix gives the aggregation rule and per-task counts. Baselines. We consider three categories of baselines in Table 1, following the evaluated configurations in RoboMME (Dai et al., 2026). VLA baselines directly predict actions from their inputs: π0.5 (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) uses the current observation without historical context, while π0.5 w/ action history additionally includes past actions in its language input (Dai et al., 2026). Memory-augmented policies equip action models with mechanisms for retaining and using history. SAM2Act (Fang et al., 2025) uses memory bank and memory attention to condition waypoint prediction on past observations; FrameSamp+Modul (Dai et al., 2026) samples historical frames and uses their visual features to modulate the action expert. Hierarchical policies separate high-level subgoal planning from low-level execution. SimpleSG+QwenVL generates language subgoals, whereas GroundSG+Gemini and GroundSG+QwenVL use grounded subgoals to specify execution targets (Dai et al., 2026). MemER (Sridhar et al., 2025) maintains selected historical keyframes as visual context for subgoal prediction. We evaluate SERA, which organizes VLM planner through an editable harness for task-context management and execution-driven selfevolution. We use gpt-5.6-sol through Codex as the high-level VLM planner, with reasoning effort set to high. 4.2 AGENTIC PLANNING How does agentic planning perform on manipulation tasks requiring historical information? Table 1 shows that the complete SERA framework achieves 51.38% overall success, compared with 42.38% for MemER and 44.51% for FrameSamp+Modul. SERA obtains the highest scores among the listed methods on Reference and Permanence, which require using earlier observations to resolve task-relevant information beyond the current view. These results suggest the potential of organizing high-level VLM as an agent for history-dependent manipulation. Within the Reference suite, VideoPlaceOrder illustrates how demonstration understanding and sustained context management support execution (Figure 3b), even without self-evolution. In this episode, the instruction specifies the second target visited in the demonstration. The robot must identify that historical target and place the blue cube at its current location. The agent identifies the intended target by interpreting the demonstrations visit order and subsequent target swap. The harness retains this information across grasp attempts while task context is updated with execution feedback. Once grasping is confirmed, the agent combines the retained target information with the current observation to locate the destination and complete placement. The execution trace separates two kinds of information: the destination inferred from the demonstration remains available through initialization guidance, while task context records whether grasping has succeeded. Subsequent planning therefore combines persistent task goal with changing execution state. The full demonstration is not supplied again at each planning round in this run. We next examine whether execution experience can improve planning guidance and control rules. 4.3 EXECUTION-DRIVEN SELF-EVOLUTION Can execution-driven self-evolution repair limitations in the initial harness and improve task performance? 7 Preprint Table 1: RoboMME main results. SERA is grouped with hierarchical policies. Baselines use official leaderboard results; SERA uses autonomous selection. Feedback obtained from execution provides an opportunity to identify where these limitations affect task performance and to revise the corresponding parts of the harness. With execution-driven self-evolution, SERA improves overall success from 44.38% to 51.38%, gain of 7.00 percentage points (Figure 3a). Revisions address inconsistent spatial interpretation, insufficient checks before advancing task stages, and missing action candidates, improving performance on tasks such as SwingXtimes and PatternLock. Figure 3c illustrates how these issues are identified and addressed through harness self-evolution on PatternLock. Analysis of failed execution reveals an incorrect mapping between visual directions and executor commands, together with candidate set that omits required action. Self-evolution corrects the direction guidance and candidate restriction, enabling the agent to complete the demonstrated sequence using existing executor actions. The revision history also shows how verifier feedback guides subsequent changes. On the same six-episode revision panel, the initial harness succeeds in two episodes. first revision targeting direction interpretation succeeds in three, but inspection of remaining failure reveals that required direction is absent from the retrieved candidates. second revision addresses this remaining issue by making all eight existing directional commands available to the planner. With this revised candidate set and the direction guidance, the harness succeeds in five of the six episodes. These are pre-test revision results, illustrating how an incomplete repair can be refined through rollout feedback; they do not constitute an isolated comparison of the two repair components. 4.4 FURTHER IMPROVEMENTS AND DISCUSSION What further improvements could help our agentic planner translate high-level decisions into more reliable task execution? One direction is to extend the harness with mechanisms that can intervene more directly in execution when replanning is insufficient. Exploratory RoboMemArena (Lei et al., 2026) evaluations motivate this direction. In task requiring two pours followed by placing the container in rack, the planner requests the second pour, but the executor places the container in the rack. Although task context retains the unfinished requirement, subsequent regrasp attempts fail. This observation suggests that maintaining the intended task state could be complemented by mechanisms for correcting execution deviations. Preprint Figure 3: Self-evolution results and complementary execution cases. (a) RoboMME success rates before and after harness revision. (b) VideoPlaceOrder: the base agent analyzes demonstration to identify the intended target despite swap, then uses retained task context to predict its current location and successfully place the cube. (c) PatternLock: self-evolution diagnoses direction-mapping errors and missing action candidates, revises the direction guidance and candidate set, and the revised agent successfully completes the sequence. VideoPlaceOrder shows test episode; PatternLock shows self-evolution repair example. Direction guides and candidate colors are schematic; paths show motion and target order. Exploratory gripper interventions provide an initial indication of this possibility. Some development runs complete the task with the intervention when matched runs without it fail, while another remains unsuccessful. These interventions operate beyond the scope of our current planner-side harness. The mixed outcomes observed across these runs indicate that achieving reliable recovery remains an open problem for this setting. Future work could investigate how an agentic planner can select and assess execution-level interventions, connecting its task understanding with more effective recovery.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented SERA, self-evolving robotic agent for history-dependent robotic manipulation that organizes high-level VLM within an editable harness around fixed VLA executor. The harness manages task context during execution, while self-evolution uses development-time execution experience to revise planning guidance, assessment criteria, and control rules. The selected harness is fixed before held-out testing. On RoboMME, autonomous SERA achieves 51.38% success, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. These results support further investigation into how the organization and adaptation of the high-level planner can contribute to VLA-based robotic control over long execution horizons. Limitations and future work. VLM reasoning introduces planning latency into the execution loop. Repeated inference over observations and task context can accumulate substantial overhead during long-horizon execution, potentially limiting timely responses in dynamic tasks. The resulting trade-off between reasoning quality and execution responsiveness remains to be systematically evaluated. Future work will investigate more efficient context processing and reasoning strategies to reduce planning latency while preserving decision quality. 9 Preprint AI USE STATEMENT We used large language models as assistive tools to help collect related literature, assist with code writing and experiment organization, and support manuscript drafting and language editing through discussions with the authors. The authors carefully reviewed and checked AI-assisted work at each stage. The core research ideas were developed by the authors, who made the final decisions and take responsibility for the final content of the paper.

(5) Suite-level scores use the same rule restricted to the four tasks in that suite. Since each task has the same number of episodes, task averaging and episode pooling coincide. Scores are computed before rounding for display. On RoboMME, autonomous SERA selects intervention bundles before test evaluation. The selection includes candidates passing development and fresh-validation checks, as well as terminal development fallbacks allowed by the procedure in Section 3.3. Tasks without selected intervention retain the base result. Selected candidates remain in the aggregate even when their test score decreases; they are not replaced after observing test outcomes. The comparison therefore reflects the selection procedure as applied, rather than per-task maximum over base and adapted test results. sections.title: B HARNESS IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: B.1 ROBOMME COMMAND INTERFACE The command catalog is extracted from released executor training labels. Each entry specifies skill identifier, an exact language template, its grounding-point count, and recorded task and transition statistics. The base retrieval scheme first restricts candidates to the known tasks entries when available. It combines rankings for the preceding skill, recorded successors, and skill frequency using reciprocal-rank fusion, supplying the top five candidates or all candidates if fewer are available. This scheme does not use semantic query similarity, even though the retrieval interface accepts text. The VLM selects catalog entry and copies its template. Each required grounding point includes an object description, source front-camera frame, and integer coordinates normalized to [0, 999] along each image axis. The harness checks the template, point count, coordinate bounds, and frame validity before rendering the command. For example, the catalog contains pick up the peg at <point 1>; subsequent hooking template requires points for the cube and its destination. These are catalog examples, not measured trajectory outcomes. Zero-point templates require no grounding points. The VLA retains its native task-goal and observation interface. In the RoboMME driver, this includes current front/wrist images, proprioceptive state, and the executors image/state buffer. This buffer is distinct from the recent visual window supplied to the high-level planner. The command interface does not establish physical success; execution evidence is processed in the next planning round. B.2 CONTEXT STATE AND RUNTIME CONTROL For RoboMME, episode initialization processes the instruction and initial context using benchmarkprovided task-specification priors. Synchronized frontand wrist-camera observations supply scenelevel and local interaction evidence during execution. The RoboMME base planner emits rewritten progress summary bounded to 1,600 characters. Its prompt requests the current phase, completed steps, task state, physical state, execution state, and material uncertainty. Structured execution fields also describe the held object, object support, and gripper state. These values are model estimates. The description and guidance obtained at episode initialization remain fixed, while the runtime summary and control state are updated and reset between episodes. Execution status distinguishes progressing, completed, uncertain, stagnant, and regressed outcomes, with separate initial status. Harness-maintained counters track repeated lack of progress and stagnation. In the catalog-only base configuration, they select normal planning, reconsideration of the current state, or renewed selection among known commands. The counters are not counts of verified task-completion events. The action-specific visual check is advisory within the same VLM call; it has no independent Python-side veto over the visual judgment. Subsequent runtime control determines the effective command and context stored for the next round. B.3 DEVELOPMENT SELECTION AND REVISION SCOPE Offline failure analysis may use benchmark-internal traces or expert demonstrations in addition to recorded planner and execution data. These are diagnostic materials: deployed revisions must express their activation conditions using task identity and runtime-observable information. The autonomous selection protocol permits both candidates passing development and freshvalidation checks and terminal development fallbacks. In the reported protocol, fallback with one additional successful episode and no observed regression can be retained for selection after searchbudget exhaustion. task with no selected intervention retains its base result. The deployed version records the selection route; the aggregate is not restricted to candidates passing fresh validation. panel containing only baseline failures cannot establish retention of previously successful episodes. Candidate manifests describe task scope, activation conditions, components, and revision lineage. The checked runtime loads prompt guidance, criterion overlays, and control rules into their corre16 Preprint sponding harness operations. The manifest format also defines broader extension types, but their presence in the schema does not establish that they were executed: in particular, the checked runtime rejects unregistered Python intervention plugins. We do not treat this interface as evidence of unrestricted online code modification.
